title: Photocatalytic nitrogen reduction to high-concentration ammonia via interfacial evaporation
source: Nature Sustainability
abstract: Photocatalytic nitrogen reduction reaction (PNRR) offers a potentially sustainable route for green ammonia (NH3) synthesis, but its practical implementation is limited by sluggish N2 and active hydrogen (*H) supply, high reaction barriers and product inhibition from NH3 accumulation on the catalyst surface. Here we show a cyanobacteria-inspired photocatalytic–photothermal interface that integrates PNRR with solar-driven interfacial evaporation (SDIE), coupling NH3 synthesis with in situ product separation. The resulting PNRR–SDIE platform accelerates reaction kinetics and mass transport while continuously removing NH3 from the catalytic interface, yielding an NH3 concentration of 2,462.38 µmol l−1 in the collected condensate water under simulated solar irradiation, 5.43–6.27 times higher than in conventional PNRR systems. Mechanistic studies reveal that the synergistic triple-phase interface and localized photothermal heating lower the activation energy for N2 reduction and facilitate reactant transport, while rapid NH3 desorption and evaporation suppress product inhibition and sustain continuous synthesis. We further demonstrate the practical utility of this platform for enhancing Brassica rapa growth using the generated NH3, establishing a closed-loop route from solar energy to NH3 and agricultural productivity. This work provides a strategy for coupling photocatalytic synthesis with interfacial evaporation for decentralized solar production and simultaneous separation of molecular products.

title: Local coordinated bismuth single-atom molecular catalyst drives bias-free photoelectrochemical plastic waste upcycling to organosulfur
source: Matter
abstract: Transforming plastic waste into valuable organosulfur chemicals, this work presents a solar-driven, continuous-flow photoelectrochemical platform. Centered on a bismuth single-atom molecular catalyst with precision-engineered local coordination, the system uniquely enables selective carbon-sulfur bond formation via a controlled interface microenvironment, establishing an efficient and bias-free route for sustainable plastic upcycling.

title: Spatiotemporal intensity-cycling microscopy unveils many-body interactions and correlated transport in van der Waals semiconductors
source: Nature Materials
abstract: Spatiotemporal optical microscopies are powerful tools to image the propagation of energy carriers in materials, including electrons, excitons, magnons and polaritons, providing key functional metrics inaccessible to contact-based transport measurements. Nevertheless, these approaches do not distinguish single-particle from multi-particle quantum states, hindering the study of many-body correlations that underlie the complex phase diagrams at the heart of contemporary materials research. Here we extend a concept derived from multidimensional spectroscopy, called intensity cycling, to the spatiotemporal domain using transient scattering microscopy. We leverage this approach to selectively image single-particle and multi-particle transport in van der Waals semiconductors. We demonstrate a series of sought-after capabilities, including clean isolation of single-particle charge transport with high signal-to-noise ratio, spatiotemporal tracking of exciton–exciton annihilation, high-throughput mapping of dielectric disorder, and imaging the emergence of a polaronic Mott transition and correlated transport in a superatomic solid. This work delivers a precision tool capable of visualizing how many-body interactions shape material function.

title: Into the Infinite Possibilities: Omar Yaghi’s Vision for Science in the Era of AI
source: National Science Review Advance Access
abstract: 2025 Nobel Laurent Omar Yaghi is establishing a new center in Tsinghua University, aiming to transform chemistry and materials science through AI and robotics.

title: Spaceborne radiation-tolerant atomic-layer memory with on-orbit real-time testing
source: National Science Review Advance Access
abstract: The human endeavor in space exploration has never ceased, where space electronics with high radiation tolerance are of paramount importance. Due to the atomic-level thin-layer characteristic, atomic-layer material electronic devices exhibit extremely high radiation tolerance compared with traditional bulk material devices. However, on-orbit testing on atomic-layer electronics is still lacking, restricting the understanding of their online performance in the space environment. Here we report a spaceborne radiation-tolerant and low-noise atomic-layer MoS2 memory array. Deployed on the Fudan No.1 Satellite in a low Earth orbit, this work enables the first demonstration of on-orbit real-time testing on atomic-layer memory. To date, after 23 months of on-orbit testing, the accuracy of the returned memory data has remained at 100%, indicating impressive radiation tolerance. This work presents a substantial step forward for the practical application of atomic-layer space electronics.

title: In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering
source: Nature
abstract: Circulating concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are leading risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease1. Despite several approved lipid-lowering medications, most patients fail to achieve target lipid levels under the chronic care treatment model2,3. Here, we describe a potential single-course treatment in which an infusion of guide RNA and mRNA encoding a CRISPR adenine base editor—encapsulated within a GalNAc–lipid nanoparticle—leads to durable, liver-selective inactivation of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANGPTL3), a known driver of increased LDL-C and triglyceride concentrations. Analyses in human liver cells in vitro confirmed that the base editor introduces a DNA base-pair change at the target ANGPTL3 locus with no detectable off-target editing at any of approximately 3000 candidate sites or treatment-related structural variants. Targeted ANGPTL3 inactivation in nonhuman primates was well-tolerated and led to a > 90% mean reduction in circulating ANGPTL3 protein, with durability confirmed out to 3 years following a single dose. In mouse and nonhuman primate models of hyperlipidemia, gene inactivation was associated with reductions of approximately 40 to 50% in LDL-C and 50 to 70% in triglycerides. These results provided the scientific foundation for initiation of an ongoing first-in-human clinical trial in patients with refractory hyperlipidemia syndromes.

title: Cyclic tetracoordinate borons enable tetrasubstituted axially chiral alkenyl silanes
source: Chem
abstract: A Pd-catalyzed atroposelective ring-opening coupling of cyclic tetracoordinate borons affords tetrasubstituted axially chiral alkenyl silanes while retaining the boron moiety. The reaction integrates boron and silicon within a configurationally stable chiral framework and exhibits broad functional-group tolerance. More broadly, this strategy expands the reactivity of tetracoordinate borons beyond conventional migration pathways and provides a distinct approach to tetrasubstituted axially chiral molecules.

title: In situ CAR engineering and nanoparticle-mediated TREM2 degradation for macrophage reprogramming in malignant ascites
source: Nature Materials
abstract: Peritoneal metastasis (PM) and the resulting malignant tumour ascites characterize advanced gastrointestinal cancers, often leading to poor prognosis and limited response to current therapies. Single-cell analysis of patient-derived PM and malignant tumour ascites reveals an approximately 90% enrichment of TREM2+-tumour-associated macrophages, which drive CD8+ T cell dysfunction and tumour growth. Here we develop lipid nanoparticles encapsulating mRNA to reprogram these tumour-associated macrophages into chimeric antigen receptor macrophages targeting Claudin18.2-positive tumour ascites. The lipid nanoparticles incorporate a TREM2+ ligand to enhance the targeting of TREM2 macrophages. The piperazine-containing phosphoramide ionizable lipid synergizes with the TREM2 ligand to inhibit ligand dissociation, promoting TREM2 internalization and degradation via lysosomal and autophagosomal pathways. This inhibits AKT signalling and reprograms tumour-associated macrophages towards an antitumour phenotype, enhancing progenitor exhausted and effector memory CD8+ T cell responses, altering the PM transcriptome, and reducing immunosuppression in both malignant tumour ascites and tumours. Combined with PD-1 blockade, this therapy suppresses tumour growth and extends survival in mice, and with matching immunological effects in clinical samples, demonstrates its translational potential for PM immunotherapy.

title: Self‐Assembled Macrocyclic Nanocarriers for Rapid Ratiometric Loading and Dosing of Multidrug Combinations
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Screening optimal drug combinations and dosing ratios is crucial for achieving and maximizing the synergistic therapeutic benefits in combined treatments. Traditional drug loading methods lack the precision to control drug ratios or involve complex technologies, failing to meet the demands of large‐scale screening in accuracy, convenience, and applicability. To address this, we developed a thermodynamically programmable macrocyclic nanoplatform based on amphiphilic calixarenes that overcomes the kinetic limitations on drug loading accuracy and reproducibility. This platform achieved precise drug loading and release with convenient tunability and broad‐spectrum applicability. For a series of drugs across various ratios, the actual loading ratio is > 95% consistent with the assigned values, and the consistency in delivery into cells and tumor tissues is also > 95%, enabling physicochemical control over the combination ratios. This work illustrates a feasible paradigm to screen for optimal drug ratios, providing a high‐throughput approach for advancing combinatorial therapeutics.

title: In Situ Bulk Passivation and Carrier Transport Modulation in Te‐TeOx Films Enable Low‐Noise Monolithic Near‐Infrared Imagers
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Near‐infrared (NIR) imagers are essential for applications ranging from material sorting and autonomous driving to biomedical diagnostics, yet their performance is often limited by severe carrier recombination and high dark current. Here, we demonstrate a low‐noise NIR photodiode based on Te‐TeO
                    x
                    nanocrystalline‐in‐matrix films, in which the surrounding oxide matrix provides in situ bulk passivation and enables the modulation of carrier transport to balance carrier loss and extraction. This approach reduces trap density, suppresses recombination, and prolongs carrier lifetime, while controlled oxide incorporation tunes the optical bandgap and interfacial offsets of the heterojunction photodiode, resulting in spectral response spanning the visible and NIR regions with low dark current. The resulting photodiodes exhibit a low dark current of 9.70 nA cm
                    −2
                    at a bias of −10 mV, a detectivity of 3.85 × 10
                    12
                    Jones and an ultralow detectable power of 1.35 pW for NIR photodetection. The strategy is compatible with direct monolithic integration with readout integrated circuits, enabling a 256 × 256 focal‐plane imager with excellent pixel uniformity. It further supports high‐quality focal‐plane imaging in both visible and NIR regions, as well as solution identification and imaging through smoke.

source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Biological signals are inherently weak and susceptible to noise, making in situ signal amplification critical for high‐fidelity sensing. Electronic fibers offer unique advantages for conformal and scalable biointegration; however, fiber amplifiers are seldom reported due to the lack of suitable semiconducting materials that combine balanced ambipolar transport, scalable fiber fabrication, and high device performance. Herein, we report the first single‐component ambipolar fiber platform based on a newly designed polymer, P(gTDPP‐TQ), which combines balanced p‐ and n‐type transport, low‐cost synthesis, and continuous fiber fabrication. These fiber amplifiers enable high‐fidelity electroencephalogram signal amplification over 20 times and sensitive cortisol sensing with a record‐low detection limit of 3.7 fM. This work establishes a general ambipolar fiber platform for integrated bioelectronic amplification and sensing.

title: Smart Luminescent Materials: From Basic Luminophores to Stimuli‐Responsive Luminescent Systems
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Smart luminescent materials (SLMs) represent an emerging class of intelligent optical systems that can convert external stimuli into adaptive and programmable photonic outputs. By integrating molecular photophysics with dynamic structural regulation, SLMs enable precise modulation of emission intensity, wavelength, polarization, lifetime, and energy conversion pathways with high spatiotemporal controllability. Recent advances in molecular engineering, supramolecular assembly, and hierarchical material design have driven a transition from conventional luminescence switching toward multifunctional systems featuring multilevel, multistimulus, and information‐enriched optical responses. This review provides a comprehensive and mechanism‐oriented overview of recent progress in SLMs across diverse material platforms, including solution‐phase systems, solid‐state materials, dynamic hydrogels, chiral circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) systems, and lanthanide‐doped upconversion nanoparticles. Particular emphasis is placed on how external stimuli regulate excited‐state electronic structures, molecular conformations, supramolecular organizations, and hierarchical architectures to achieve adaptive luminescent behaviors. In addition, emerging strategies for stimuli‐responsive CPL regulation and intelligent photon conversion based on upconversion nanomaterials are highlighted, demonstrating how molecular‐level control can be translated into dynamic optical functionalities. Finally, current challenges and future opportunities are discussed toward the rational design of next‐generation smart luminescent materials for applications in information security, wearable electronics, soft robotics, biophotonics, and intelligent photonic devices.

title: Cross‐Scale Decoupling of Mechanics and Kinematics in Chiral Tensegrity Metamaterials
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Compression‐torsion metamaterials (CTMs) that break spatial inversion symmetry face persistent trade‐offs among large deformation capacity, intrinsic stiffness, and fatigue durability. Crucially, boundary rotation induced by axial compression complicates integration with rotationally constrained engineering interfaces. Here we introduce a chiral three‐rod tensegrity cell (CTTC) paradigm that addresses these conflicts through a cross‐scale dual‐decoupling strategy. First, mechanical decoupling at the unit‐cell scale separates macroscopic shape‐morphing from large local material strain: a heterogeneous rigid‐flexible architecture channels global compression into kinematic rod displacement and uniform elastic‐network stretching, achieving 97° torsion at Level 0 and only 4.87% peak‐force degradation over 10 000 cycles at Level 3. An integrated geometric interlocking reconfigurator further enables post‐fabrication programmability of stiffness and strain‐normalized twist ratio (
                    R
                    T‐S
                    ). Second, kinematic decoupling at the assembly scale localizes torsional deformation as a boundary‐decoupled internal rotational mode, while maintaining external interfaces in pure translation. This cross‐scale framework establishes a deployable paradigm bridging metamaterial physics and robotic systems operating in geometrically constrained environments.

title: In Situ Probing of Small‐Molecule Electrolysis Using Ambient‐Pressure X‐Ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Electrocatalytic small‐molecule conversion addresses the need to couple renewable electricity with sustainable fuel and chemical production, yet challenges remain in resolving the dynamic gas/solid/liquid interfaces that govern catalytic activity, selectivity and stability. A key challenge is to correlate catalyst structures, reaction intermediates and local interfacial environments under comparable operating conditions. Ambient‐pressure x‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (APXPS) provides surface‐sensitive and chemically specific information on catalyst chemical states, interfacial species and local electrostatic environments at the same working interface, enabling direct correlations between catalyst evolution and reaction intermediates. We offer a forward‐looking review of APXPS for probing gas/solid/liquid interfaces in small‐molecule electrolysis. We discuss three categories of electrochemical XPS/APXPS configurations: quasi‐in situ XPS, in which electrochemically treated catalysts are transferred under protected conditions for post‐reaction analysis; thin‐electrolyte‐film (dip‐and‐pull) APXPS, which probes a potential‐controlled interface through a nanometer‐scale liquid film; and membrane‐based APXPS, which accesses catalyst–ionomer–electrolyte interfaces. We introduce present‐day challenges in electrochemical APXPS and describe a vision towards more realistic operating conditions, higher time resolution and multimodal measurements integrated with theoretical and data‐driven spectral analysis. These developments provide potential avenues to establish reliable structure–intermediate–environment relationships in the further development of small‐molecule electrocatalysis.

ABSTRACT
                  
                    The controlled growth of two‐dimensional (2D) non‐layered transition metal oxides remains a key challenge in low‐dimensional material synthesis. Achieving atomically precise construction of 2D structures requires a fundamental understanding of how external fields and interfacial interactions govern nucleation and growth processes. title: Electrochemical Indicators for Designing Durable Low‐Pt Fuel Cell Catalysts
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Improving the durability of platinum (Pt)‐based catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) remains a central challenge in the commercialization of proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), yet simple and effective indicators to guide the rational design of highly stable Pt‐based catalysts are still lacking. Herein, we identify initial electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) and dry proton accessibility (DPA) as two key indicators for unraveling cathodic Pt/C catalyst degradation. Systematic studies on a library of Pt/C catalysts with a wide range of initial ECSA (49–114 m
                    2
                    g
                    Pt

                    ) and DPA (27%–91%) reveal clear relationships between these two indicators and ECSA loss: at a comparable DPA, ECSA loss decreases significantly with the reduction in initial ECSA; at a similar initial ECSA, lower DPA effectively mitigates ECSA loss; and the influence of DPA on ECSA loss becomes increasingly prominent as initial ECSA decreases. Regression analysis further clarifies the respective roles of these two indicators: initial ECSA is the dominant factor associated with ECSA loss within the catalyst library, while DPA further modulates degradation depending on the initial ECSA level. These findings suggest that catalyst durability can be improved by prioritizing the reduction of initial ECSA, with further benefits achieved by lowering DPA.

title: Cathode‐Driven Aluminothermic Fronts Amplify Thermal Runaway in Lithium‐Ion Batteries
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Thermal runaway in lithium‐ion batteries often develops from a local failure into a spatially propagating high‐temperature front. Here, we show that oxygen‐bearing cathode materials and metallic aluminium can form self‐sustained, glowing, cathode‐driven aluminothermic fronts in inert gas as a heat‐amplification pathway relevant to severe thermal runaway. Using a mesoscale platform based on semi‐1D composite bars, we isolate this interfacial redox chemistry from gas‐phase combustion, internal short‐circuit heating, and other coupled cell‐failure processes. Nickel‐rich layered oxide/aluminium bars sustain aluminothermic‐front propagation in argon, with velocities of the same order of magnitude as reported thermal‐runaway fronts. By varying aluminium loading, reaction atmosphere and cathode chemistry, we show that front propagation depends on aluminium fuel supply, the oxygen‐donor capability of the cathode, and access to oxygen gas. Crystalline phase and chemical‐state analyses reveal Li–Al–O/Al–O products together with reduced or reconstructed transition‐metal species, supporting cathode‐to‐aluminium oxygen transfer as the underlying redox pathway. For a representative 2‐Ah cell, energy‐audit calculations indicate that the aluminium‐cathode reaction gives a potential heat scale equivalent to about half of the stored electrical energy. These findings identify cathode‐Al redox chemistry as an internal heat‐amplification mechanism that should be considered in battery hazard assessment and high‐energy‐cell safety design.

                    exhibits excellent chemical‐ and photo‐stability even after 40 days of water soaking and 14 days under natural sunlight, or under high‐light intensity up to 2 suns for 120 mins. The high stability of
                    PBQ
                    is attributed to extensive delocalisation of the spin density across its large π‐conjugated backbone and the presence of stabilising heteroatoms. Additionally,
                    PBQ
                    exhibits photothermal power generation and simultaneous cogeneration of steam and electricity. This work demonstrates an imidazole‐linked diradicaloid as a high‐performance photothermal material, offering a molecular platform for solar‐driven water purification and energy conversion.

title: Ionization‐State‐Directed Sulfonate‐Rich Buried Interfaces Enable Durable High‐Efficiency Perovskite Solar Cells and Modules
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Proton‐triggered degradation at the buried interface severely undermines the operational stability of inverted perovskite solar cells (PSCs). To address this issue, this work develops an ionization‐state‐directed sulfonate approach using sodium 2,2'‐disulfanediyldiethanesulfonate (DDANA). The pre‐deprotonated sulfonate terminals grant DDANA strong coordination with lead sites and drive its spontaneous aggregation at the perovskite and self‐assembled monolayer interface, forming robust multisite binding with the perovskite lattice. The enriched sulfonate groups build favorable interfacial dipoles to optimize energy level alignment and facilitate hole transport. The immobilized sulfonate groups act as conjugate‐based sites to competitively capture protons, while the disulfide skeleton enables reversible iodine‐redox to scavenge corrosive iodine species under operational stress. Dissociated sodium (Na
                    +
                    ) ions embed into lattice interstices and release residual tensile strain. As a result, DDANA‐modified inverted PSCs achieve a champion efficiency of 27.38% (certified 27.13%). The strategy extends seamlessly to flexible devices and rigid large‐area modules, delivering efficiencies of 25.88% and 23.33%, respectively. Moreover, the DDANA‐modified devices retain 98.9% of their initial efficiency after 1000 h of maximum power point tracking and 97.4% after cycling diurnals. This work establishes sulfonate ionization‐state engineering as a versatile molecular design platform for constructing chemically robust buried interfaces toward efficient, stable, and scalable perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Heterostructure Design in Two‐Dimensional Perovskites by Sequential Recrystallization
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Low‐dimensional metal halide perovskites provide exciting opportunities to fabricate new semiconductor materials. Semiconductor technology relies on electronic heterojunctions, and cost‐efficient and flexible approaches to realize functional heterostructures are of fundamental importance. Lateral heterostructures define the energy landscape in the plane of the semiconducting lattice in 2D perovskite materials, representing an ideal platform to tailor energy barriers and to control charge carrier flow. Here, we demonstrate a versatile one‐pot synthesis to fabricate a large variety of 2D perovskite heterostructures based on different halides and/or metal cations. Exploiting sequential crystallization of different 2D perovskites and tuning the composition and injection events of the materials, enables the design of diverse heterostructure architectures, including multiple heterojunctions. We obtain heterostructures with high crystalline quality, multicolor emission, and optical coupling between the different heterostructure regions. We foresee that the design freedom of our method will stimulate the development of novel optoelectronic devices where electronic band engineering is crucial.

title: Conjugation Interruption in 1D COFs for Boosted Charge Separation and Photocatalytic 2,3‐Dihydrobenzofuran Synthesis
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are appealing photocatalyst platforms because of their structural designability and tunable optoelectronic properties. However, the traditional strategy of extending π‐conjugation to improve light absorption often increases exciton binding energy and suppresses charge separation, creating a trade‐off that limits catalytic performance. Here, we introduce a conjugation‐interruption strategy for the first time to construct efficient COF‐based photocatalysts, where methylene (sp
                    3
                    ) bridges are incorporated into one‐dimensional (1D) framework backbones to moderately disrupt long‐range conjugation, localize electrons and reduce exciton binding energy. Schiff base condensation of the 4‐connected thiadiazole‐containing tetra‐aldehyde with 2‐connected angular diamine precursors consisting of naphthyl, phenyl, and methylene bridges afforded BT‐NDA‐COF, BT‐TDA‐COF, and BT‐MDA‐COF, respectively. BT‐MDA‐COF with the weakest conjugation, exhibits the longest fluorescence lifetime (1.57 ns) and the lowest exciton binding energy (63.21 meV), clearly outperforming its fully conjugated counterparts (BT‐TDA‐COF and BT‐NDA‐COF). Combined experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that the methylene bridges induce structural distortion and weaken exciton confinement, thereby promoting charge separation. This superior charge separation enables gram‐scale photocatalytic synthesis of bioactive 2,3‐dihydrobenzofurans with 98% yield, demonstrating the practical potential of conjugation interruption in COFs for green, high‐efficiency photocatalytic organic synthesis.

title: ZrO2 Clusters Enabling Room‐Temperature Hydrogen Absorption and Low‐Temperature Desorption of Commercial Mg Powder for Reversible Hydrogen Storage
source: Wiley: Advanced Energy Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Magnesium‐based hydrogen storage materials exhibit great application potential, but high operating temperature and slow kinetics hinder their large‐scale utilization. Here, the amorphous‐carbon‐stabilized Mg particles decorated with sub‐2 nm ZrO

title: Orchestrating Tumor‐Immune Interface and Microenvironment Remodeling via a Tumor‐Preferential DNA Nano‐Regulator for Metabolic‐Immunotherapy
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Metabolic reprogramming in malignant cells drives tumor progression and impairs immunotherapy efficacy, highlighting the urgent need for synergistic metabolic‐immunotherapy. However, the pharmacokinetic disparity and systemic toxicities pose significant challenges on this synergy. We develop a tumor‐preferential, multifunctional DNA nano‐regulator assembled on a DNA origami‐based framework with two functional layers for the integration of immune cues and metabolic modulation at the tumor‐immune interface. The inner layer is precisely functionalized with anti‐CD3/CD28/PD‐L1 antibodies and glutamine synthetase, enabling in situ T‐cell engagement, PD‐L1 blockade, and metabolic environment improvement. The outer layer combines albumin‐binding domains with pH‐responsive i‐motif switches to form a pH‐sensitive albumin coating in vivo, which shields the inner antibodies during systemic circulation and specifically exposes them within the tumoral acidic microenvironment. In the xenograft and syngeneic mouse models, the regulator‐mediated broad remodeling of the intratumoral immune and metabolic landscapes results in enhanced T‑cell infiltration and activation, potent tumor‐growth suppression, and a favorable safety profile. This study combines metabolic intervention with immunotherapy by integrating the synergism and tumor preference of therapies.

title: Heterometallic Polarization Enabling Precise Intermediate Regulation for Selective CO2 Photoreduction
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT

Here we introduce a heterometallic polarization strategy based on bimetallic metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), where asymmetric charge redistribution between distinct metal centers tailors the local electronic structure and modulates CO* binding energetics. Taking MIL‐88A(Fe/Ni) as a model system, the incorporation of Ni induces intermetallic electronic coupling, creating polarized Fe─Ni sites that synergistically enhance CO

title: Ionomer‐Free Iridium Anodes With Low Loading for Zero‐Gap Electrolyzers via Direct Atomic Layer Deposition
source: Wiley: Advanced Energy Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) is among the most promising techniques to provide hydrogen as both energy carrier and feedstock for the chemical industry, due to its compatibility with intermittent renewable electricity sources. However, a major bottleneck in scaling up PEMWE is the limited supply of the anode catalyst Ir. This work shows a novel approach to tailoring ionomer‐free catalyst layers based on custom‐made microporous substrates and two different atomic layer deposition (ALD) processes, both using Ir(EtCp)(CHD) precursor. Thermal ALD using  as counter‐reactant yields mostly metallic Ir/ and an electrode Ir loading of 0.21 . The PEMWE cell‐level performance is comparable to a commercial catalyst‐coated membrane anode despite  lower loading, and is maintained over an accelerated durability test equivalent to 600 h of intermittent operation. Moreover, using a low‐loading ALD‐made cathode, the total platinum group metal loading is only 0.24 . Plasma‐enhanced ALD reduces the Ir loading to 0.04  by tailoring the catalyst distribution, however, yields lower‐activity . Finally, direct ALD catalyst deposition needs no ionomer‐bearing ink. The anodes are therefore compatible with various membrane materials, as demonstrated in a  electrolysis experiment with an anion exchange membrane.

title: Synergistically Modulating Electronic Structure and Interfacial Wettability of MnF2/NF−CNF Toward Enhanced Oxygen Reduction in Zinc−Air Batteries
source: Wiley: Advanced Energy Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Modulating the electronic structure and interfacial wettability of cathode catalysts is crucial for enhancing intrinsic activity and broadening triple‐phase interfaces for oxygen reduction reactions (ORR) in zinc−air batteries (ZABs), yet achieving their synergistic regulation faces a big challenge. Herein, an N/F source modulation strategy is proposed to synthesize porous carbon nanofibers anchored with MnF
                    2
                    nanocrystals and N/F heteroatoms (MnF
                    2

                    2

                    −2

                    2

Meanwhile, surface F dopants, in synergy with the porous architecture, regulate wettability, equilibrate electrolyte/oxygen transport, and substantially extend triple‐phase reaction interfaces. The assembled ZAB delivers an exceptional peak power density of 181.5 mW cm
                    −2
                    with high specific capacity, rate capability, and cycling stability. This work deciphers the regulatory mechanism balancing catalytic activity and interfacial wettability, proving a versatile strategy for developing advanced ORR electrocatalysts in ZABs.

source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Mechanically interlocked structures (MIS) provide a powerful platform for creating advanced materials with unprecedented topological architectures. Nevertheless, current related studies have predominantly focused on the construction of MIS with single topological motifs, and the integration of multiple topologies into a single MIS remains a grand challenge. Herein, we harness ligand conformational constraints to regulate the flexible coordination behavior of alkali metal ions, enabling the construction of a multi‐topologically superposed mechanically interlocked polymer (

                    MIP

This work breaks the boundaries of conventional MIS by enabling the creation of multi‐topologically superposed MIS, thereby unveiling new topological landscapes and opening unexplored opportunities for advanced functions.

title: Tailored Cationic Visible‐Light‐Active Interfaces for Sustainable, Biodegradable Nanofibers With Dual‐Mode Antimicrobial Activity and Robust Electrostatic Particle Capture
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  The accumulation of microplastics originating from single‐use personal protective equipment presents a growing environmental concern. Developing biodegradable fibrous alternatives is essential, but integrating robust antimicrobial efficacy with stable electrostatic capture while maintaining degradability remains a critical challenge. Here, we report a surface co‐functionalization strategy addressing these challenges through covalent immobilization of sodium copper chlorophyllin (SCC) and quaternary ammonium compounds (QAC). Beyond simple dual functionalization, this molecular design induces intramolecular charge separation, suppressing electron‐hole recombination in SCC and thereby amplifying reactive oxygen species generation under visible light. Simultaneously, QAC introduce permanent cationic surface charges that enable contact‐mediated microbial inactivation and humidity‐resistant electrostatic particle capture. Demonstrated on biodegradable silk nanofibers as a model substrate, the functionalized fibers exhibit potent antibacterial and antiviral activity under both dark and illuminated conditions, together with high nanoparticle capture efficiency. Importantly, the fibers retain intrinsic biodegradability, undergoing near‐complete degradation under enzymatic conditions and substantial decomposition in soil environments. This work establishes a versatile surface functionalization platform applicable to diverse fibrous substrates, offering a sustainable alternative to conventional microplastic‐generating protective materials.

title: Interface‐Confined Cationic Polarization Enables Rapid and Reversible Polyiodide Conversion for High‐Rate Zinc–Iodine Batteries
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Aqueous zinc–iodine (Zn–I
                    2

Many cathode‐regulation strategies improve iodine chemistry through physical confinement and polar adsorption. However, simultaneously suppressing polyiodide shuttling and enabling rapid iodine conversion remains challenging, particularly under high‐rate where fast interfacial redox kinetics are required. Here, interface‐confined cationic polarization is established by integrating π‐delocalized guanidinium cations (Gdm
                    +

                    2

                    +

This work demonstrates interface‐confined cationic polarization as an effective strategy for regulating polyiodide redox chemistry, offering a new route toward high‐rate and long‐life Zn–I
                    2

abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Two‐dimensional (2D) conjugated polymer single crystals are highly desirable for optoelectronics, yet their realization is limited by the intrinsic coupling between molecular‐weight buildup and chain entanglement, which disrupts long‐range order. Here, we report a gas–solid interfacial polymerization strategy that decouples monomer diffusion from chain propagation, enabling the growth of quasi‐2D polyphenylacetylene (PPA) single‐crystalline nanoribbons on Cu/CuO

This process is likely enabled by surface coordination‐assisted activation of phenylacetylene and directional π‐stacking‐driven assembly, which suppress chain entanglement and promote crystallographic ordering. As a result, micrometer‐scale PPA single‐crystalline nanoribbons with left‐handed cis‐transoidal helical chains and long‐range crystallinity are obtained. title: Rigid Double‐Spiro‐Grid Polymer Regulates Donor Fibrillar Pre‐Assembly and Acceptor Interdiffusion in Layer‐by‐Layer Organic Solar Cells
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Layer‐by‐layer (LBL) fabrication of organic solar cells (OSCs) decouples donor and acceptor deposition, which, however, induces difficulties in controlling donor crystallization and acceptor interdiffusion. Here, we introduce NPSG, a fully conjugated double‐spiro‐grid polymer, to regulate donor fibrillar pre‐assembly before acceptor deposition. Morphological results reveal that NPSG shifts D18 assembly from loosely associated aggregates toward pronounced fibrillar pre‐assemblies in solution. Molecular dynamics simulations further suggest that the rigid NPSG backbone provides multiple noncovalent interaction sites that favor anisotropic association between D18 chain segments. During film formation, these fibrillar precursors evolve into a coherent and solvent‐resistant donor framework, which moderates L8‐BO interdiffusion and promotes a vertically graded, double fibrillar heterojunction. The resulting morphology facilitates interfacial charge transfer, improves the balance of electron and hole transport, and suppresses nongeminate recombination. Consequently, the optimized D18+NPSG/L8‐BO devices achieve a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 21.2%, with a certified value of 20.7%. This strategy also improves device reproducibility, processing tolerance, applicability across different donor/acceptor systems, and operational stability under maximum‐power‐point (MPP) tracking. These findings establish donor‐underlayer pre‐assembly regulation as an effective strategy for efficient and robust sequentially processed OSCs.

title: Twistsonics: Engineering Acoustic Topological Textures in Moiré Sound Lattices
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Moiré superlattices formed by twisting periodic systems provide a powerful platform for emergent topological phenomena, but their use for programming real‐space topology in acoustic wave fields remains largely unexplored. Here, we report a phase‐controlled spoof surface acoustic wave platform for constructing moiré topological textures in the acoustic particle‐velocity field. On a perforated acoustic metasurface, two twisted skyrmion lattices are synthesized and superposed, yielding acoustic skyrmion bags with controllable topological numbers and geometries. The twist angle and rotation center control the scale and configuration of the bags, enabling deterministic reshaping of the composite texture. We further introduce controlled defects to assess the defect tolerance of the moiré skyrmion bags. The skyrmion bags retain their composite topology over a finite range of defect fractions, and comparison with an untwisted single‐layer skyrmion lattice suggests enhanced stability of the enclosed skyrmion cluster relative to the single‐layer reference at higher defect fractions. The same programmable platform also supports transitions from skyrmion lattices to meron lattices and enables twist‐induced meron clusters. These findings establish acoustic moiré superlattices as a reconfigurable platform for engineering robust real‐space topological textures, with potential applications in topology‐guided acoustic manipulation and information encoding.

title: Design of Heteroatomic Active Sites for Electrochemical COx Reduction Toward Multicarbon Products
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    The electrochemical CO

Although Cu catalysts exhibit unique activity, these single‐metal sites are constrained by linear scaling relations of intermediate adsorption energies, which limits further improvements in selectivity and energy efficiency. Introducing heteroatoms to regulate active‐site coordination provides an effective approach to transcend these limitations. This review describes recent advances in the theoretical design, controllable fabrication, and mechanistic investigation of heteroatomic active sites for CO

Then, the precision synthesis strategies for constructing atomically dispersed, long‐range‐ordered, and interfacial‐confined heteroatomic structures are systematically summarized. Subsequently, mechanistic insights into the promoting effect of heteroatoms, driven by synergistic electronic and geometric modulation, are highlighted, followed by an analysis of future research directions and the key challenges for the industrial implementation of heteroatomic catalysts for CO
                    x

title: Mevalonate pathway regulates double-negative regulatory T cell stability in metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Lipid metabolism dysfunction and immune imbalance are critical pathogenic drivers of metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Double-negative regulatory T cells (DNTreg) are important immune regulatory cells that maintain liver immune homeostasis. However, their survival and function are compromised in MASLD. Herein, we found that mevalonate pathway and its rate-limiting enzyme HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR) were significantly down-regulated in DNTreg from both mice and patients with MASLD, correlating with impaired DNTreg viability and immunosuppressive function. Arachidonic acid is enriched in MASLD liver and inhibits DNTreg HMGCR expression. Geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP), a downstream product of HMGCR, mediates RAC1 geranylgeranylation, which facilitates its interaction with mitochondrial CLPX protease, thereby enhancing mitochondrial function and immunoregulatory activity of DNTreg. Adoptive transfer of
                    Pggt1b
                    +/−
                    DNTreg into MASLD mice demonstrated significantly diminished therapeutic efficacy compared with wild-type DNTreg. In conclusion, mevalonate metabolism–mediated geranylgeranylation is essential for the suppressive activity and immune homeostasis of DNTreg in MASLD.

title: Electron competition in azobenzene programs infection-adaptive antibacterial therapy
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Conventional stimulus-responsive antibacterial systems generally operate through binary trigger–activation mechanisms, making them poorly suited to evolving infection microenvironments and thereby contributing to persistent infection and resistance development. Here, we establish an azobenzene-based kinetic regulatory system in which oxygen gradients commonly present in infected tissues continuously program reaction kinetics through electron competition. Oxygen acts as a competing electron acceptor within the reductive reaction network, partitioning electron transfer between azo reduction and oxygen consumption. Substituent electronic structures further reshape reduction propensity, encoding distinct kinetic behaviors. These electronically programmed kinetics translated into adaptive nanoscale dissociation and drug-release profiles: Electron-rich azobenzenes rapidly disassembled under severe hypoxia, whereas electron-withdrawing structures sustained release under mild hypoxia, generating infection state–adaptive antibacterial outputs. Moreover, the same electronic features governing reduction kinetics also reduced the reactivity and toxicity of reductive metabolites. This work establishes electron competition as a strategy for converting environmental gradients into continuous kinetic outputs for adaptive antibacterial therapy.

title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and
                    Brassica rapa
                    as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in
                    B. rapa
                    and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.

                     = −29 K). The unique nonalternant design suppresses hyperfine and vibrational decoherence, giving rise to long spin relaxation and coherence time. These findings demonstrate that embedding nonalternant motifs into PH polyradicals provides a powerful strategy to simultaneously promote molecular stability, spin-exchange coupling, and spin robustness—key features for materials in the rising field of quantum information science.

title: Ultrafast Meissner-levitated microrotor
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Levitated mechanical systems offer a powerful and flexible platform for the realization of ultralow-noise sensors and tests of fundamental physics. Here, we report the demonstration of a levitated microrotor, consisting of a magnetic microsphere levitated by the Meissner effect at 4.2 kelvin. The rotor reaches rotation frequencies above 2.3 megahertz (138 million revolutions per minute) while exhibiting an exceptionally low damping rate of 4.75 × 10
                    −7
                     hertz. Exploiting the linear dependence of friction on the gas density, we demonstrate high-accuracy absolute pressure sensing over a wide range at cryogenic temperature. Last, we detect the thermal torque noise at intermediate pressure by operating the rotor in synchronized mode, resulting in a first preliminary narrowband search for axion-like dark matter. More broadly, the combination of high rotational speed, low temperature, and low thermal torque noise establishes a previously unidentified regime for precision measurements, with direct implications for the detection of extremely weak forces and fields.

title: Shape-memory scaffold targets inflammation and fibrosis to restore endometrium and fertility in intrauterine adhesions
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Intrauterine adhesion (IUA) is a major cause of infertility, yet current treatments remain limited in preventing fibrosis and restoring functional endometrium. We report a bi-drug, bifunctional, biodegradable shape-memory regenerative (BiSMR) scaffold enabling minimally invasive implantation, sequential drug release, and barrier protection. Proteomic profiling of chemical, mechanical, and combined injury models revealed inflammatory activation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and impaired regenerative programs, providing a molecular rationale for combining epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) with 17β-estradiol (E
                    2
                    ). BiSMR couples an E
                    2
                    -loaded PLTG [poly(
                    l
                    -lactide)-
                    co
                    -trimethylene carbonate-
                    co
                    -glycolic acid] backbone with a PDA-EGCG@HAMA coating, enabling rapid EGCG release followed by sustained E
                    2
                    delivery. In vitro, BiSMR promoted cell proliferation, migration, angiogenesis, and M2 polarization while suppressing myofibroblast transition. In rat IUA models, BiSMR restored endometrial structure and vascularization, reduced fibrosis, and improved implantation and live birth rates. Proteomics revealed down-regulation of fibrosis- and inflammation-related effectors and restoration of protein biosynthesis and regenerative pathways. BiSMR offers a promising strategy for IUA therapy and fertility restoration.

title: Gastruloids reveal alternative morphogenetic routes for body-axis elongation with distinct cytoskeletal dependencies
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Morphogenesis requires cells to integrate genetic and environmental information to pattern and shape tissues. Recent studies in vivo and in vitro have shown how alterations in environmental cues can induce alternative morphogenetic programs. However, what determines which morphogenetic strategy cells deploy in different environments remains unknown. Using gastruloids, a model for mammalian posterior body-axis elongation where environmental cues can be controlled in vitro, we show that substrate availability determines which force-generation strategy cells employ to build the body axis. In free-floating conditions, gastruloids self-assemble a single posterior body axis, presumably through cell–cell interactions. When plated on laminin, gastruloids acquire a flat morphology, break symmetry multiple times, and produce several independently elongating cell streams with anterior–posterior polarity through collective cell migration. On laminin, formin activity and focal adhesion-mediated traction are required for tissue elongation, yet both are functionally dispensable in free-floating conditions. Transcriptomic analysis shows that formin inhibition blocks elongation on laminin without any detectable transcriptional changes, indicating that these cytoskeletal components play primarily a mechanical role that is only required when cells engage a substrate. Furthermore, laminin biases cells toward posterior migratory fates while preserving similar Hox expression. Together, these results show that mammalian body-axis elongation can proceed through different morphogenetic modes that engage distinct mechanical effectors depending on substrate availability. These findings have implications for understanding how evolution explores morphological diversity and how tissue engineering might achieve desired forms through precise environmental control.

title: Temporal dynamics of antigen-specific T cell expansion in primary SARS-CoV-2 infection
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Quantifying T cell response during primary infection in humans is crucial for understanding adaptive immunity. Leveraging a controlled human challenge to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, we characterized antigen-specific T cell responses within and across individuals. Notably, individual clones reached similar maximum frequencies despite differences in the timing of their peak expansion. Mathematical modeling within a coarse-grained framework suggested that variability in precursor frequency between different T cell clones could be one mechanism to explain this relationship. Single-cell profiling revealed distinct temporal programs for CD4
                    +
                    and CD8
                    +
                    T cells, with CD4
                    +
                    cells expanding earlier but contracting to a lower frequency. Clones with similar receptors, likely recognizing the same antigen, expanded at similar times. Together, these findings highlight how clone-intrinsic properties such as precursor frequency and CD4/CD8 subset status shape T cell clonal kinetics. These insights provide a quantitative framework for understanding T cell response in humans, with implications for vaccine design.

title: Evolutionary dynamics of collective behavior across the tree of ray-finned fishes
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Trait evolution and lineage diversification are thought to be driven by selection on the phenotypes of individuals. However, many important phenotypes are only manifested when individuals interact. Collective behavior is one such phenotype. During collective behavior, interactions among individuals lead to emergent group-level phenotypes that can govern individual fitness. Yet, whether collective behaviors exhibit similar patterns of trait evolution to individual traits and whether these group phenotypes have influenced macroevolutionary diversification is unknown. In ray-finned fishes, the most species-rich of all vertebrate classes, many species exhibit striking displays of collective behavior in the form of collective movement. Here, we use state-of-the-art machine learning methods for text and image analysis to quantify collective movement phenotypes for 2,839 Actinopterygian fishes, comprising nearly 10% of all extant species. We find that collective movement is highly evolutionarily stable in some clades and extremely labile in others, exhibiting over 300 evolutionary transitions. Consistent with theoretical predictions, collective movement is associated with more patchy diets and higher predation pressure. Finally, we find that the evolution of collective movement coincides with an increase in net macroevolutionary diversification rate. Our analyses reveal that collective behavior is deeply intertwined with ecological and evolutionary dynamics across a vast phylogenetic scale, unlocking questions about the evolution of collective phenotypes and their role in shaping the diversity of life on Earth.

title: Coupling of structural preordering and density fluctuation: A unified picture of nucleation in metallic glasses
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Crystallization is ubiquitous in nature and technology, occurring in pharmaceuticals, biomacromolecules, polymers, metallurgy and glass formation. Yet how crystallization proceeds, particularly at its earliest stage, remains elusive. Studies on glass-forming liquids increasingly suggest that crystallization initiates in structurally preordered regions, with density fluctuations playing a secondary role, a view widely generalized from hard-sphere colloids. Here we show, across disordered metallic systems from pure elements and intermetallic compounds to glass-forming alloys, that density fluctuations and structural preordering emerge simultaneously during nucleation. This coupling reflects local atomic rearrangements in which free-volume reduction, denser packing, and bond-orientational order develop together. Our findings provide a physical basis for a unified nucleation framework for disordered materials.

title: Respiratory phase orchestrates human olfactory cortical dynamics
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Olfaction is fundamental to perception, memory, and emotion, yet the neural basis of human odor processing remains poorly understood. We demonstrate that odor-evoked brain activity is organized by respiratory phase—not absolute time—revealing that natural breathing structures olfactory cortical dynamics. Using simultaneous nasal respiration and electroencephalography recordings in
                    
                      
                        17
                      
                    
                    participants, we delivered naturalistic odors (peppermint, oregano, and grapefruit) synchronized to individual breathing cycles. Odor presentation elicited respiratory phase-locked event-related spectral perturbations (RPL-ERSPs) in frontal and temporal regions, emerging during the first breath after stimulus onset. The most discriminative neural signatures were theta-band activity during inhalation and alpha-band activity during exhalation, patterns that were obscured in traditional time-locked analyses due to natural variability in breath duration. Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation of RPL-ERSPs achieved reliable odor detection (peppermint: AUC
                    
                      
                        =
                      
                    
                    0.79; oregano: AUC
                    
                      
                        =
                      
                    
                    0.67; grapefruit: AUC
                    
                      
                        =
                      
                    
                    0.62), establishing that phase-locked features generalize across individuals. To connect neural responses to perceptual experience without relying on odor naming-which can be disproportionately impaired in some populations-we quantified odor recognition using free-response descriptions scored with a semantic-similarity approach. Behavioral recognition strength paralleled the neural decoding hierarchy across odors, establishing the perceptual validity of RPL-ERSPs. RPL-ERSPs revealed rapid habituation, with decoding performance declining over repeated presentations, due to selective degradation of the most informative phase-locked features. These findings establish respiratory rhythm as a temporal scaffold for human olfactory cortical processing, positioning RPL-ERSPs as a sensitive, task-free approach for assessing olfactory function. We provide an open-source, respiration-synchronized olfactometer design to enable replication and adoption.

title: Identification of a specialized lipid barrier for Drosophila metamorphosis
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Many terrestrial insects transition from humid to dry environments at metamorphosis, yet how they avoid dehydration is unclear. In
                    Drosophila melanogaster
                    , we identify a lipid barrier to water loss in the pupa that is anatomically distinct from that of the adult. It comprises unisex hydrocarbons that are longer and less volatile than their sex-specific adult counterparts. These hyperlong hydrocarbons are produced by larval oenocytes and stored in the fat body for subsequent transport to the cuticle at pupariation. A fatty acid elongase, EloHL, is required for hyperlong hydrocarbon biosynthesis and for a functional barrier to dehydration during early metamorphosis. Hyperlong barrier hydrocarbons are widespread across the
                    Drosophila
                    genus and typically transition to shorter sex-specific versions during adult maturation. In the desert species
                    D. mojavensis
                    , however, adults retain hyperlong hydrocarbons. This study reveals how insect lipid barriers are tuned to environmental variations in aridity and temperature during development and evolution.

title: Spatial proteomics reveals lipid droplet reorganization in symbiotic Paramecium bursaria cells
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Endosymbiosis is an important adaptive mechanism allowing organisms to exploit previously inaccessible niches. The flexible relationship between the ciliate
                    Paramecium bursaria
                    and green algae represents a model system for studying early endosymbiosis evolution. However, the mechanisms underlying how
                    P. bursaria
                    cells maintain this endosymbiotic relationship remain unclear. Here, we use mass spectrometry–based proteomics to generate a spatial proteomic atlas of the host
                    P. bursaria
                    cells with and without endosymbionts. This atlas defines the protein composition of the endosymbiont-containing compartment (perialgal vacuole) and reveals pronounced remodeling of host lipid droplets upon symbiosis. Imaging analyses confirm that lipid droplets change in size, morphology, and positioning, accumulating near intracellular algae. Perturbing symbiotic cells with chemical inhibitors of lipid metabolism reduces endosymbiotic algal numbers, revealing a role for lipid droplets in the host-endosymbiont interaction. Our data provide a comprehensive resource for protein localization in
                    P. bursaria
                    cells and elucidate how those cells remodel an existing cellular compartment to maintain endosymbiosis.

title: Comprehensive degron mapping in human transcription factors
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Gene expression is regulated by the targeted degradation of transcription factors through the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Transcription factors destined for degradation are recognized by E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases through motifs termed degrons, embedded within the sequence. In this study, we systematically map degrons in all 1626 human transcription factors. We find thousands of both known and previously unidentified degrons and characterize their sequence properties. Active degrons placed within exposed and intrinsically disordered regions contribute to modulating the abundance of the transcription factors, while the most common somatic mutations that are linked to skin cutaneous melanoma lead to unfolding and exposure of a latent degron buried in the zinc finger structure. We present examples of compartment-specific degrons and demonstrate that variant effects in transcription factors correlate with degron potency. Last, we show that while >60% of all predicted transcriptional activation domains overlap with strong degrons, acidic residues within the remaining transactivating regions counter the degron potency, showing how degrons can shape the transcription factor sequence landscape.

title: Spatial control of enzyme orientation at the lipid droplet interface enables regio- and chemoselective metabolic flux
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Precise spatial control over multienzyme cascade reactions is increasingly recognized as a design lever in synthetic biology for enhancing catalytic performance and directing metabolic flux. By emulating principles of cellular compartmentalization, synthetic scaffolds and engineered interfaces have emerged as powerful platforms to modulate intermediate channeling and reaction efficiency in complex biocatalytic systems. However, robust and spatially defined immobilization of multienzyme assemblies within physicochemically optimal compartments remains challenging because of the dynamic intracellular environment. Here, we reprogram the amphiphilic interface of yeast lipid droplets (LDs) as a programmable scaffold system to support regio- and chemoselective localization of enzymes. Guided by molecular dynamics simulations, we designed LD-anchoring motifs to direct the enzyme orientation at the LD monolayer interface, yielding cytosol-facing or LD inner-facing configurations. Using this designed LD-anchoring motif, we spatially reorganize a trienzyme cascade for prodeoxyviolacein (PDV) biosynthesis across the cytosol-LD interface, facilitating directional conversion of hydrophilic substrates into hydrophobic products. This spatial reorganization substantially improved PDV production by 1300%, achieving 46.25 milligrams per liter. Our approach offers a modular and tunable platform for engineering spatially organized and readily deployable enzyme cascades, opening avenues for biosynthetic catalysis at organellar interfaces.

title: Measuring mixed-state topological invariant in open photonic quantum walk
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Pure-state manifestations of geometric phase are well established and have found applications across essentially all branches of physics, yet their generalization to mixed-state regimes remains largely unexplored experimentally. The Uhlmann geometric phase offers a natural extension of pure-state paradigms and can exhibit a topological character. However, observation of this invariant is impeded by the incompatibility between Uhlmann parallel transport and Hamiltonian dynamics, as well as the difficulty of preparing topologically nontrivial mixed states. To address this challenge, we report an experimentally accessible protocol for directly measuring the mixed-state topological invariant. By engineering controlled nonunitary dynamics in a photonic quantum walk, we prepare topologically nontrivial mixed states from a trivial initial state. Then, by machine learning the full density matrix in momentum space, we directly extract the quantized geometric phase of the nontrivial mixed states. Furthermore, we observe that this transition of the quantized mixed-state topological invariant from a trivial to a nontrivial value is closely associated with the emergence of a topological kink structure. These results highlight a geometric phase framework that naturally extends to open quantum systems both in and out of thermal equilibrium.
